reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Severe multisystem malformation syndrome caused by an extra copy of chromosome 13, with high perinatal and infant mortality
Midline defects are characteristic, including holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, and midface anomalies
Postaxial polydactyly, clenched hands, and rocker-bottom feet are typical limb findings
Ocular anomalies such as microphthalmia or anophthalmia and scalp defects (cutis aplasia) are helpful clues
Major congenital heart defects are present in most affected infants
Caused most often by full trisomy 13 from meiotic nondisjunction, with risk rising with maternal age
A minority of cases result from a Robertsonian translocation, which carries recurrence implications for the family
Mosaic forms can produce milder, more variable phenotypes
reference.pathophysiology: Patau syndrome arises from an extra copy of chromosome 13, most commonly a full trisomy caused by maternal meiotic nondisjunction, with incidence increasing with maternal age. Around a fifth of cases result from an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 13, and a smaller proportion from mosaicism. The surplus chromosome 13 material disrupts embryonic development, particularly midline structures of the brain and face, producing holoprosencephaly and associated craniofacial defects, along with cardiac, renal, and limb malformations. The severity of central nervous system and cardiac anomalies underlies the very high mortality.
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray to confirm trisomy 13 and detect translocation or mosaicism
Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing including cell-free DNA and invasive confirmation when indicated
Cranial imaging to assess for holoprosencephaly and other brain anomalies
Parental karyotyping when a translocation is identified
redFlags: Severe cardiac and central nervous system malformations causing early life-threatening instability
Recurrent apnoea, seizures, and feeding failure requiring goals-of-care discussion
Higher recurrence risk in translocation cases, making parental testing important
Need for early, compassionate counselling given the poor prognosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is very poor, with most infants dying in the first days to weeks of life and few surviving beyond the first year, typically with profound disability; mosaic forms may have a better outlook.
pitfalls: Not distinguishing full trisomy from mosaic or translocation forms, which affects counselling
Failing to arrange parental karyotyping when a translocation underlies the case
Overlooking comfort-focused care needs while pursuing investigations
Missing associated anomalies such as holoprosencephaly on imaging
